The feature maps in the qualitative analysis are taken just before the $1\times1$ convolution ToRGB block that generates the SR image. **W1. In the quantitative comparison with SOTA methods, the proposed LaUD model does not consistently demonstrate a clear advantage. This raises questions about the practical benefits of adopting LaUD over simpler or more established models, especially given the additional complexity introduced by the LP-based detail control and RUDP.**

We would like to provide a few points to further clarify and highlight the strengths of our approach.

First, we acknowledge that our model performs poorly for 8x SR on Urban100, and we think it requires an analysis of the reasons. However, apart from the case of 8x SR on Urban100, we do not consider the improvements achieved by our model to be negligible. Excluding this particular case, LaUD demonstrates a noticeable improvement of approximately 0.2–0.3 dB in PSNR in most cases over CNN-based models. Notably, many models in Table 1 achieve only a 0.2–0.5 dB improvement compared to the previous year's model. Moreover, our approach consistently outperforms some attention-based models such as RCAN, ABPN, DRLN, and HAN. These results highlight the practical effectiveness of our proposed RUDP and LP-based detail loss.

Next, the main points we tried to convey in our paper are 1) the LP-based detail loss is an effective technique for improving SR models, and 2) RUDP generates a synergistic effect with the detail loss, rather than directly introducing the LaUD model itself. To validate these, we applied our methods to several attention-based models, extending beyond the CNN structure, and demonstrated that our methods can also achieve performance improvements in attention-based models.

Finally, we believe that the additional complexity introduced by our method, particularly for the detail loss, is minimal. In the case of detail loss, the number of parameters and memory usage of the model remain almost unchanged, as the only additional step involves extracting one more image during the upscaling process. This is supported by the comparison table in the appendix A.5.3 that we added in our revised draft. It provides details on the number of parameters, memory usage, training time, and inference time. In the case of RUDP, we acknowledge that it increases the model's complexity to some extent. However, we believe it is difficult to conclude that LaUD has greater complexity compared to other models. Many models introduce additional complexity to improve performance, such as employing sophisticated attention mechanisms or incorporating an iterative upscale-and-downscale approach similar to RUDP.

First and foremost, we would like to clarify that "RDUP," as mentioned by the reviewer, is a typo and should be "RUDP." We apologize for the confusion and have corrected this error.

Regarding the abbreviations, many of the abbreviations we used—HR, LR, SR, LP, and SOTA—were chosen because we believed they were not excessive and would be familiar to most readers. However, we recognize that RUDP (Repeated Upscaling and Downscaling Process) and LaUD (Laplacian pyramid-based Upscaling and Downscaling Super-Resolution Network) are terms we introduced. Based on the reviewer's feedback, we agree that including the full forms at the beginning of each new section could be helpful for clarity. Unfortunately, doing so would exceed the length limit of the main text, so we decided not to make this modification. We kindly ask for your understanding.

**W5. The efficacy of Laplcian Pyramid in the field of SR was already explored in the popular work,"Deep Laplacian Pyramid Networks for Fast and Accurate Super-Resolution". The authors should have framed their work on this approach and try to compare and prove how their approach was better than this.**

First, we would like to point out that LapSRN was mentioned in the related work section of the original draft, along with a brief comparison (L149). As noted in that section, while LapSRN introduced a reconstruction structure based on the Laplacian Pyramid (LP) similar to ours, a significant difference lies in the way we introduce the detail loss. Providing a more detailed discussion of LapSRN could indeed be helpful. However, in the main results, we chose to compare our model with DRLN, which more recently introduced LP concepts and demonstrated better performance than LapSRN. Furthermore, due to space constraints, we decided not to include an additional comparison with LapSRN. We kindly ask for the reviewer's understanding.

**W6. As loss function is their main contribution, the authors should try to compare their approach with other loss functions commonly use din SR.**

Although we did not directly compare variations of the loss function, the ablation study comparing the inclusion and exclusion of our detail loss was included in Table 2 of our original draft. It provides insight into the differences between the standard $L_{1}$ loss for SR, commonly employed in SR tasks, and our proposed loss function, which combines the $L_{1}$ loss for SR with our detail loss. As shown in the comparisons of No. 1 and No. 4, No. 2 and No. 5, and No. 3 and No. 6 in Table 2, the models utilizing our loss function consistently demonstrate higher performance.

In addition to $L_{1}$ loss, other types of loss functions commonly used in SR tasks include $L_{2}$ loss and perceptual loss. Generally, $L_{2}$ loss for SR performs worse than $L_{1}$ loss, so it can be inferred that $L_{2}$ loss would also perform worse than our proposed loss, which demonstrates higher performance than $L_{1}$ loss for SR. From this perspective, experiments using $L_{2}$ loss for SR were not conducted. However, an experiment was carried out with a slight modification to our loss function, and we added the results in the appendix A.5.2 of our revised draft. Specifically, this experiment involved a model that retained the $L_{1}$ loss for SR while replacing the $L_{1}$ loss for detail with the $L_{2}$ loss for detail. As shown in the appendix results, using $L_{1}$ loss for detail consistently demonstrated higher performance compared to $L_{2}$ loss.

**Weaknesses:**

**W1. Though, the authors show different experiments to prove the efficacy of their approach, but the contributions of the work are too limited for acceptance.**

While we understand the reviewer's concern regarding the scope of contributions, we respectfully believe that our proposed approach introduces meaningful advances in SR research. The experiments in Section 4 demonstrate its effectiveness in the SR problem for various datasets. We hope this addresses the reviewer's concerns.

**W2. What is the exact difference between the upscaled and detail feature shown in fig. 1a. How can the authors prove that they are actually learning different meaningful information, and not increasing redundancy. The authors can show feature Map visualisations.**

In response to the reviewer’s concern, we have added additional analysis with example images of the upscaled feature and detail feature in the appendix A.6.2. However, we'd like to provide a further explanation for this below for your reference.

Although we derived a detail feature from the upscaled feature and combined them to form the SR feature, the detail feature exhibits distinct characteristics compared to the upscaled feature, since both the SR feature and detail feature are guided respectively by $L_{1}$ loss and detail loss. In detail, through our analysis of feature maps, we observed that the detail feature frequently contains information about boundaries and textures, including details that are absent in the upscaled features. On the other hand, the upscaled feature map predominantly retains complete object structures, and consists of features with varying contrasts. This is the biggest difference between the detail and upscaled features. This difference is consistently observed in our feature map comparisons across various experimental results. At present, there is no solid theoretical foundation to support it. However, the consistent findings across multiple observations have made our analysis of the detail feature more reliable.

Next, for the actual learning of the detail feature map, our analysis reveals that it contains meaningful information and plays a distinct role in the creation of SR features. The results in the appendix A.6.2 provide two examples illustrating the role of the detail feature map. First, the detail feature map reinforces insufficient high-frequency information in the upscaled feature map by leveraging its prominent boundaries and texture information. Second, it adjusts excessively flat values in the upscaled feature map. Consequently, the SR feature exhibits greater value curvature and seems to capture a more dynamic and lively appearance.

**W3. How does the author finalise the number of levels (3) in their designed model. The authors should have included an ablation study for them.**

Experiments on the number of repetitions of upscaling and downscaling process were conducted but were not included in the main paper. These results have now been added to the appendix A.5.1.

Regarding the selection of three RUDP, this decision was made based on experimental results rather than a theoretical basis. As shown in the experiments on the number of RUDP, which have been added in the appendix, we observed that the performance improved as the number of RUDP increased. Also, we observed that the performance gains became negligible after four repetitions (this specific experiment was not documented). Additionally, as the number of RUDPs increases, the resources required for training, such as memory, also increase. Repeating the upscale and downscale process more than four times posed a risk of memory limitations for our current computing resources. Therefore, we aimed to select a configuration that achieved high performance while staying within resource constraints, ultimately setting the number of repetitions to three.

In Figure 1-(b), $H_{Down_{1}}$ concatenates with $I_{LR}$ in “concat” box. **Q2. The authors state that significant structural changes to the proposed RUDP are necessary in some cases to apply the LP-based detail loss to attention-based models (L255-256). If such changes hinder the effectiveness of the detail loss, it suggests that there may be substantial limitations in applying the proposed loss function to other models. The reviewer would appreciate the authors' perspective on this issue.**

We want to clarify a few points that may have contributed to the reviewer's confusion.

First, we want to highlight that using only LP-based detail loss is also effective in improving model performance. While RUDP can deform the structure, detail loss does not cause significant changes. As shown in the results in Table 2, the highest performance is achieved when RUDP is used together with detail loss. However, detail loss alone is still sufficiently effective. Therefore, when applying our method to improve the performance of other existing models, we believe that applying only detail loss is not a bad idea if deformation is a concern.

Next, applying RUDP is straightforward, except when integrating it into an existing model with minimal changes to the original architecture. In our experiments with attention-based models using our methods, we aimed to minimize modifications to the existing architectures, which introduced certain limitations. However, if one intends to apply RUDP while designing a model from scratch, one can simply incorporate the downscale process after the SR image generation step and repeat the preceding upscale process.


**Q3. In Figure 3 and Figure 11, comparisons are made only with DBPN, DRLN, and SwinFIR. Could the authors clarify why these specific methods were chosen? Would it be possible to include comparisons with all the methods shown in Table 1? Let us first address why specific models such as DBPN, DRLN, and SwinFIR were chosen for comparison. In the image comparison experiments, only a subset of models was selected, as is common in similar studies, since comparing all the models listed in Table 1 would require excessive space. Among the models in Table 1, DBPN was selected as a CNN-based model that introduces a technique similar to ours, DRLN was chosen as an attention-based model with a comparable technique, and SwinFIR was included due to its high performance as an attention-based model. Additionally, models with open-source code available were prioritized for practical reproducibility.

Regarding the inclusion of comparisons with all the methods shown in Table 1, we believe this would be challenging due to space limitations in the main text, and we are also concerned about overcrowding the appendix. Therefore, we will include and share the results of all models in Table 1 on GitHub, which will be released later.

For Figures 3 and 11, analyzing cropped sections is a conventional method in SR research. This approach helps analyze the structures or details where a model shows high performance within an image. Thus, comparing the entire image before zooming does not align with our analysis intent, and we have decided not to include it in Figures 3 and 11.

However, comparing the entire image before zooming is a useful method for evaluating the overall performance of the model. Due to space limitations, they will be made available on our GitHub at a later date, not in this draft.

**W4. The effectiveness of the methods proposed in this paper remains uncertain. In Table 1, LaUD demonstrates only slight improvements over CNN-based models, with PSNR gains of around 0.1 in many cases. First, we would like to emphasize that our model showed a larger difference of 0.2 to 0.4 dB in most cases compared to the CNN-based models, rather than just 0.1 dB. Our model consistently achieved higher results, except in two cases: for 8x SR on Urban100, where its performance was relatively lower, and for 4x SR on Urban100, where it underperformed only compared to HBPN. It demonstrated differences of at least 0.2 dB on Set5, Set14, 2x SR on BSD100, and 2x SR on Urban100. As mentioned in our response to W1, we believe this difference is meaningful, as many models typically show improvements of 0.2 to 0.5 dB compared to models from the previous year.

In addition, while the performance drop in the 8x SR on Urban100 should be thoroughly analyzed and addressed for improvement, our model outperformed RCAN, DRLN, ABPN, and HAN among the attention-based models in all cases except for the 8x SR on Urban100. Therefore, the statement that 'LaUD consistently lags behind attention-based methods' is incorrect.
So, we think the effectiveness of the methods proposed in this paper is presented sufficiently.

Our perspective on the ablation study aligns with the response provided in W1. While the differences in PSNR based on the presence or absence of each component are relatively small, they are nonetheless significant when considering typical PSNR differences in SR tasks. Thank you for your valuable feedback. We respond to the concerns that you have raised below.

**Weaknesses:**

**W1. The authors claim that rather than generating $H_{U_{k}}$ and $H_{D_{k}}$ in parallel within the upscaling block, producing $H_{D_{k}}$ from $H_{U_{k}}$ allows the model to capture high-frequency information that may otherwise be missing (L219-L222). As the reviewer mentioned, the content in lines L219-L222 lacks sufficient evidence and is more akin to a conjecture. However, we wrote this way because we analyzed the feature maps that were not included in the original draft. When we examined the feature map $H_{D_{k}}$, derived from $H_{U_{k}}$, we observed that certain boundaries and textures emerge due to the influence of the detail loss. It seems that these boundaries correspond to the boundaries of objects in $H_{U_{k}}$. Consequently, when $H_{U_{k}}$ and $H_{D_{k}}$ are combined, a more informative $H_{SR_{k}}$ is generated. (We revised our draft to contain more explanation about this analysis with images in the appendix A.6.2.) The statement in the current draft is written based on this reasoning. However, the statement may sound too strong without mentioning the additional experiments described here. Instead of providing more experimental results and their analysis that could support the original statement, we decided to modify the statement in the revised draft.

In response to the concern regarding Table 2, our thoughts are as follows. First, for PSNR, the difference between the model with all components—RUDP, weighted sum, and detail loss (No. 6)—and the one without these components (No. 1) is approximately 0.24 dB in PSNR. We believe this difference is not insignificant. For example, in Table 1, for 2x SR on Set5, the difference between the smallest and largest performance values is approximately 1 dB, and many models show only a 0.2–0.5 dB improvement compared to the previous year's model. In this context, we believe our 0.24 dB difference is meaningful. Next, when only one method is introduced (e.g., No. 3 vs. No. 6, or No. 5 vs. No. 6), the difference seems relatively small. However, even in such cases, differences of about 0.1 to 0.2 dB are observed, with consistent trends overall. We believe this clearly demonstrates the effectiveness of each technique.

Regarding the statement, “Higher values in these metrics (PSNR and SSIM) do not necessarily indicate effective capture of high-frequency information”, although these metrics may not directly measure the effective capture of high-frequency information, we used PSNR and SSIM because they are widely recognized as representative indicators of image quality. In general, high image quality in SR tasks often correlates with more accurate restoration of high-frequency details, which is why we considered these metrics as proxies for capturing high-frequency information. While we are not aware of other specific metrics designed for this purpose, we would use and compare the results if there are any well-known alternatives commonly discussed in the field.

summary.value: This paper introduces the Laplacian pyramid-based Upscaling and Downscaling Super-Resolution Network (LaUD), a CNN-based model designed for super-resolution tasks. The proposed LaUD uses a repeated upscaling and downscaling process (RUDP), which repeats downsampling the completed SR feature map and combining it with the LR image to extract new upsampled approximation and detail features. summary.value: This paper proposes a new image super-resolution technique that can independently generate super-resolution images and detail images. This method improves image quality by independently generating super-resolution images and detail images. This technology uses a loss function based on the Laplacian pyramid to optimize high-frequency details and improve the quality of super-resolution images. The loss function is constructed based on the Laplacian pyramid, which is suitable for cyclic upsampling and downsampling operations.

strengths.value:
1. The proposed Laplacian pyramid (LP) detail control loss method enables the model to independently process high-frequency information in detail images, thereby focusing more on the details and supplementing missing information in upsampled images.

2. This paper validates the effective combination of RDUP (repeated upsampling and downsampling) and LP based detail control. The experiment shows that RDUP can capture more diverse information by re-extracting detail information from SR features.

weaknesses.value:
1. The parameters related to the method in the paper should be marked in Figure 1 for the convenience of readers to read.
2. The comparison between the formula and the architecture diagram in Figure 1 is not rigorous, for example, Hn=Hn-1+Resn (Hn-1), n=1,2.., N. Please modify the diagram or formula. In addition, it is necessary to add a serial number after the formula to facilitate readers' reading.
3. The author's modeling approach using selective generation is similar to many early methods, with comparable effectiveness: DRRN and NAFNet, especially NAFNet achieved SOTA results in 2022 with extremely low parameter count. However, the author did not compare this type of algorithm. Please add comparative experiments with this type of algorithm to verify the superiority of the proposed iterative method.
4. The paper introduces the Laplacian pyramid method as a loss to enhance the details of super-resolution images. However, there are too few relevant descriptions in the results images and loss functions sections. Please supplement the process and formula for obtaining images as labels. Although the author shows the process of the Laplacian pyramid in the supplementary materials and mentions the use of supervised learning for learning, this is not consistent with the detail maps shown in the subjective comparison results. Please display the detail labels used in the supervisor comparison results.
5. This article uses a simple CNN network with detail loss to achieve more competitive results. Theoretically, this simple network is also more competitive in terms of parameters, computational complexity, and running time. Please include a comparison of parameters, computational complexity, and running time in the comparison results.
6. This article proposes the RUDP module for restoring detailed information on images. Is there any theoretical basis for the proposed LaUD using RUDP twice? Can using it more times achieve better results? Please demonstrate in the ablation experiment.

summary.value: This paper proposes a super-resolution model using a novel detail control loss based on the Laplacian Pyramid and a repeated upscaling and downscaling process to enhance high-frequency details in images. The authors demonstrate their approach by implementing a new CNN-based model, LaUD, which achieves competitive performance metrics and is tested on multiple datasets. Furthermore, they apply the LP-based detail loss to attention-based SR models and report minor improvements. The experiments show promising quantitative results, indicating that the proposed techniques can be applied across various SR models.

strengths.value:
1. Introducing LP-based detail control loss is a notable idea that targets high-frequency information, which is essential for image super-resolution.

2. The proposed method is tested on both CNN and attention-based models, showcasing its adaptability to different architectures.

weaknesses.value:
1. In the quantitative comparison with SOTA methods, the proposed LaUD model does not consistently demonstrate a clear advantage. While the model performs competitively, the improvements in PSNR and SSIM are modest, particularly when compared to established models. For instance, in the 8× upscaling scenario on Urban100, LaUD’s performance lags behind that of several attention-based models. This raises questions about the practical benefits of adopting LaUD over simpler or more established models, especially given the additional complexity introduced by the LP-based detail control and RUDP.

2. While the ablation study shows that RUDP and LP-based detail control positively impact the performance, it lacks a thorough exploration across different datasets and SR scales. More diverse conditions could substantiate the robustness of these components. The authors do not investigate the trade-offs introduced by adding the detail control loss in terms of computational cost, memory usage, or training time, which would be valuable for a practical assessment of its viability.

3. Although the quantitative results are presented, the difference in metrics between LaUD and SOTA models is small, which may not justify the complexity of adding both LP-based detail control and RUDP. The qualitative analysis of feature maps is difficult to interpret in terms of real-world impact. The authors could provide further explanation or visualization to clarify how these enhanced high-frequency details manifest in output quality.

4. Certain aspects of the methodology, particularly in adapting LP-based detail loss to attention models, lack clarity. Specific details about modifications required for each model, especially regarding architectural changes, are crucial for reproducibility but are only briefly addressed, with many descriptions deferred to the appendix.

questions.value:
1. Could you provide a comparison of model size, memory usage, and inference time between LaUD and the other state-of-the-art models?

2. Could you provide more experimental data in the ablation section to show a comparison of the proposed method’s impact on the three base models (ABPN, HAN, and DRLN)?

title.value: Detail Loss in Super-Resolution Models Based on the Laplacian Pyramid and Repeated Upscaling-Downscaling Structure

abstract.value:
With advances in artificial intelligence, image processing has also gained significant interest. Image super-resolution, in particular, is a vital technology closely related to real-life applications, as it enhances the quality of existing images. Since enhancing details is important in the super-resolution task, it is often necessary to activate pixels that appear only at high frequencies, distinct from low frequencies. 
In this paper, we propose a method that generates a detail image separately from the super-resolution image. This approach introduces a loss function designed to enhance detail, allowing the model to generate an upscaled image and a detail image independently, with control over each component. Consequently, the model can focus more effectively on high-frequency data, resulting in an improved super-resolution image. Our loss function utilizes detail images based on the Laplacian Pyramid, which is widely used in image reconstruction. The multi-level property of the Laplacian Pyramid is well-suited for applying upscaling and downscaling repeatedly.
Our experiments demonstrate that a structure applying the repetition of upscaling and downscaling integrates effectively with our detail loss control. The results show that this structure efficiently extracts diverse information, enabling the generation of improved super-resolution images from multiple low-resolution features. We conduct two types of experiments. First, we construct a simple CNN-based model incorporating the Laplacian Pyramid-based detail control and a repeated upscaling and downscaling structure. This model achieves a state-of-the-art PSNR value of 38.48 dB, surpassing all currently available CNN-based models and even some attention-based models without additional special techniques. Second, we apply our methods to existing attention-based models on a small scale. In all the experiments, attention-based models using our detail loss show improvements compared to the original models. These experiments demonstrate that our detail control loss effectively enhances performance, regardless of the model's structure in the super-resolution task.

def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
